title: The Ten Miles: Königsberg, the Silent Decade, and the Books That Traveled Instead
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Königsberg, the birth in the Vorstadt
stops.date_confidence: date attested in the parish register; the house site is reconstructed from parish and city records, not marked today, and the coordinate is quarter-level only
stops.campa: In the Vorstadt suburb south of the Pregel, in a harness maker's house near the Hospital of the Holy Ghost, a fourth child is born to Johann Georg Kant and Anna Regina Reuter. Nine children come; six reach adulthood. The register enters him as Emanuel, and he changes the spelling to Immanuel later, after he learns Hebrew. The house does not survive the city, and its plot is inferred from parish and municipal paper rather than pointed to on a street. The boy born in it will die about two miles from this point, seventy-nine years and ten months from today.
suggested_refs: Königsberg parish registers of the Vorstadt, entry for 22 April 1724
Eighteenth-century city plans of Königsberg showing the Vorstadt south of the Kneiphof

stops.name: Königsberg, the Collegium Fridericianum
stops.date_confidence: attested year of entry; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At eight he is entered in the Collegium Fridericianum, the Pietist Latin school run by Franz Albert Schultz, and stays there eight years. The regimen is prayer, self-examination, and the demand for a conversion a boy can date. Kant reacts against all of it and goes on saying so for fifty years. What he takes out of the place is Latin: the classics construed until the meter sits in the ear. British bombs destroy the building in August 1944 and the school closes in January 1945, two hundred and thirteen years after he first walked in.
suggested_refs: Engravings of the Collegium Fridericianum before its destruction in 1944
Klemme, Die Schule Immanuel Kants (1994)

stops.name: Königsberg, the death of Anna Regina
stops.date_confidence: attested; German record gives 18 December 1737, and the earlier hedge that the year was unconfirmed is struck
stops.campa: Anna Regina Kant dies on the eighteenth of December, of an illness some accounts lay to a physician's bad advice. Her son is thirteen. She had walked him out of the city to name plants and constellations, and she had carried him to the preaching of Franz Albert Schultz, who noticed the boy and saw him into the Collegium. Kant credits her, in old age, with awakening his feeling for nature and his moral seriousness. The house of a harness maker with six living children is now a house without a mother, and the Pietism she brought into it stays behind her.
suggested_refs: Borowski, Darstellung des Lebens und Charakters Immanuel Kants (1804), on the mother

stops.name: Kneiphof, matriculation at the Albertina
stops.date_confidence: attested year and month; day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: At sixteen he crosses to the Kneiphof island and matriculates at the Albertus-Universität, the Albertina. He reads philosophy, mathematics, physics, logic, metaphysics, ethics and natural law, under the physicist Johann Gottfried Teske and above all under Martin Knutzen, a Wolffian and a Pietist at once, who puts Newton into his hands and teaches him that the heavens are calculable. Kant will study at no other university. He will teach at no other university. At sixteen he has entered the institution that will hold him for sixty-four years.
suggested_refs: The Albertina matriculation register for autumn 1740
Views of the old university buildings on the Kneiphof

stops.name: Königsberg, the father's death and the abandoned degree
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1746; day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Johann Georg Kant, struck down two years before and unable to work since, dies in March. The saddler's income dies with him. Kant is twenty-two, with younger siblings to keep and a manuscript in his box on the vis viva controversy, the quarrel between the Cartesians and the Leibnizians over how force is to be measured. He argues that the two camps are measuring different things. He leaves the Albertina without taking any degree at all, and the manuscript waits three more years for a printer.
suggested_refs: Gedanken von der wahren Schätzung der lebendigen Kräfte, first edition, Königsberg 1749

stops.name: Judtschen, the pastor's sons
stops.date_confidence: post held roughly 1747 to 1750; start month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He takes the first of his tutoring posts, in Judtschen, a hundred kilometers east of the city, teaching the sons of the Reformed pastor Daniel Ernst Andersch. The parish register lists him standing godparent to village children, and that register is nearly the whole documentary record of three years of his life. While he is out here, Königsberg finally prints Thoughts on the True Estimation of Living Forces, his first book. The restored parsonage, in what is now Vesyolovka in Kaliningrad Oblast, opened as a small Kant museum in 2018.
suggested_refs: Judtschen parish records naming Kant as godparent, cited in Vorländer (1911)
The Kant museum at Vesyolovka, opened 2018

stops.name: Groß Arnsdorf, the major's estate
stops.date_confidence: post held roughly 1750 to 1753; coordinate corrected to the modern village of Jarnołtowo, about 22 km west of the figure first given
stops.campa: The second post is on the estate of Major von Hülsen at Groß Arnsdorf near Mohrungen, in the Oberland of Prussia proper and not in Warmia, which was a separate territory. Kuehn gives the major's name as Bernhard Friedrich and the Polish record of the village as Karl Friedrich; the two are left standing against each other. Almost no correspondence survives from these years, so the household, the duties and the hours are known secondhand or not at all. Jarnołtowo put up a plaque in 1994, a museum in the fire station in 2012, and a life-size Kant in 2013.
suggested_refs: The 1994 plaque and 2013 sculpture at Jarnołtowo, Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship
sources: Kuehn, Kant: A Biography (2001), citing Borowski (1804)

stops.name: Capustigall, the Keyserlingk question
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the existence of the post is disputed and the year is approximate, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Borowski and Jachmann, who both knew Kant in person, describe a third tutorship in the household of the Count and Countess von Keyserlingk, at Waldburg-Capustigall in the Pregel valley just west of Königsberg. Manfred Kuehn denies it was a tutorship at all and dates the Keyserlingk friendship after the return to the city. A German account of the estate says flatly that Kant never lived there and came out from Königsberg by the day. The accounts are not reconciled here. Either way this is the last country house that will ever hold him.
suggested_refs: Schloss Waldburg-Capustigall in the Heyde-Waldburg district west of Königsberg
Jachmann and Borowski, the two 1804 eyewitness biographies

stops.name: Königsberg, the return
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1754; month traditional, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: After some six years of other people's children he comes back to Königsberg. He is thirty. What follows is fifty years inside one city: the same island, the same lecture rooms, the same short streets between a rented room and a castle library. René Descartes had by this age lived in the Dutch Republic, wintered in Bohemia and was on his way to dying in Stockholm. Kant's entire remaining itinerary can be walked in an afternoon. The popular claim that he never went ten miles from the place again is a commonplace, not a document; what the record shows is only that no journey after this is attested.
suggested_refs: Street plan of eighteenth-century Königsberg: Kneiphof, Altstadt, Löbenicht, Vorstadt

stops.name: Kneiphof, the nebular hypothesis
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He publishes, with no name on the title page, the Allgemeine Naturgeschichte und Theorie des Himmels. The solar system condensed out of a rotating cloud of matter under Newtonian attraction. The Milky Way is a disc seen edge on. The nebulae are other such discs, island universes at distances he does not pretend to give. Laplace reaches the same mechanism forty years later and the hypothesis carries both names. The publisher goes bankrupt, most copies never reach a shop, and the cosmology attracts almost no notice for decades.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Naturgeschichte und Theorie des Himmels, Königsberg and Leipzig, 1755, anonymous first edition
sources: Kant, Allgemeine Naturgeschichte und Theorie des Himmels (1755)

stops.name: Kneiphof, the Magister and the venia legendi
stops.date_confidence: the De Igne defence is attested to April 1755 and the licence to lecture to September; days not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In April he defends De Igne, on fire, and takes the Magister degree his father's death had cost him nine years earlier. In September he defends the Nova dilucidatio on the first principles of metaphysical cognition and is licensed to lecture. A Privatdozent draws nothing from the university; he is paid coin by coin by the students who choose to sit in the room. So Kant teaches everything and teaches it constantly: logic, metaphysics, mathematics, physics, natural law, physical geography, hour after hour through the week. The system that will take reason apart is built in the margins of a teaching load carried in order to eat.
suggested_refs: Kant, Meditationum quarundam de igne succincta delineatio (1755)
Kant, Principiorum primorum cognitionis metaphysicae nova dilucidatio (1755)

stops.name: Königsberg, the Lisbon papers and the invention of a discipline
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the three earthquake papers; the geography lectures begin in 1757, month and day unknown
stops.campa: The Lisbon earthquake of All Saints' Day 1755 kills tens of thousands and shakes the theology of a continent. Kant answers with three papers in one year on the causes of earthquakes, subterranean cavities and heated gas, the shock running along the line of the great river valleys. The mechanism is wrong and the move is not: a catastrophe treated as a natural event with a natural cause. The year after, he begins to lecture on physical geography, a subject he founds as a German academic discipline and goes on teaching for the rest of his working life.
suggested_refs: Kant's three 1756 earthquake essays, cited in histories of early seismology
Kant, Physische Geographie, the lecture course as later edited by Rink (1802)

stops.name: Königsberg, the Russian occupation and the chair refused
stops.date_confidence: occupation attested 1758 to 1762; the petition is attested to December 1758, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Russian troops occupy Königsberg in the Seven Years' War. The university swears allegiance to the Empress Elizabeth, Russian officers fill the benches at his lectures, and his purse is fuller under an occupying power than it had been under his own king. In December he petitions the Empress for the vacant chair of logic and metaphysics. It goes to an older man, longer in service. He is thirty-four, teaching the whole of natural science for student fees, and the foreign sovereign who now governs his city has just declined to promote him.
suggested_refs: Kant's 1758 petition to Empress Elizabeth of Russia for the chair of logic and metaphysics

stops.name: Königsberg Castle, the first salary and the spirit-seer
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the library post, held to 1772; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He takes the post of under-librarian in the royal castle library, holds it six years, and it is the only regular institutional income of his life before the professorship. Two years earlier he had been a popular author for a season with the Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime, and had come second to Moses Mendelssohn in the Berlin Academy's prize competition. Now he publishes Dreams of a Spirit-Seer, half satire and half warning, in which the metaphysics that claims to know beyond sense is set beside Swedenborg's ghosts and does not clearly win.
suggested_refs: Träume eines Geistersehers, erläutert durch Träume der Metaphysik (1766)
The royal library in Königsberg Castle, Kant's workplace 1766 to 1772

stops.name: Kneiphof, the inaugural dissertation
stops.date_confidence: appointment and August dissertation attested; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Erlangen had offered him a professorship in 1769 and Jena a chair in 1770; he declined both without traveling to either, and waited for the one chair in his own faculty. At forty-six, after fifteen unsalaried years, he gets it. In August he defends De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis, which already divides the world as given to sense from the world as conceived by intellect, and treats space and time as the form of the first rather than properties of the second. Everything after this works out a distinction made in a Latin exercise required for a job.
suggested_refs: Kant, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis (1770)

stops.name: Königsberg, the silent decade
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the silent decade is a scholarly characterization of the years 1770 to 1781, with no single date
stops.campa: For eleven years he publishes almost nothing of consequence. He carries the full teaching load, dines out, keeps his hours, and rebuilds metaphysics from the ground; the phrase silent decade belongs to the historians and not to him, and what happened inside it is reconstructed from the result rather than watched. Nobody in Königsberg who sees the professor leave his door at the same hour each afternoon has any way of knowing that the longest deliberate silence in European philosophy is being kept behind the shutters of a rented room.
suggested_refs: Kant's correspondence 1770 to 1781, the principal evidence for the silent decade

stops.name: Königsberg, the Critique of Pure Reason
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; written in rented rooms, since the Prinzessinstraße house is not bought until 1783, and the exact address in that period is disputed
stops.campa: The Critique of Pure Reason is finished in rented rooms in the middle of the city and sent to Johann Friedrich Hartknoch in Riga. Kant does not go to Riga; the whole business passes by letter and courier. The book argues that objects conform to the mind rather than the mind to objects, and that space, time and the categories are the conditions under which anything can appear at all. It is his first book in eleven years, and it is so little understood that two years later he writes the Prolegomena, a shorter restatement, to explain what he had meant.
suggested_refs: Kritik der reinen Vernunft, Riga, Johann Friedrich Hartknoch, 1781, first edition

stops.name: Königsberg, the house on Prinzessinstraße
stops.date_confidence: attested year of purchase; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At fifty-nine he buys a house on Prinzessinstraße near the castle, the first property he has ever owned, and leaves the rented rooms where the first Critique was written. He will live here twenty-one years and die in it: a servant, a cook, a table of guests at midday, a study. The Prolegomena appears the same year he takes possession. The house is pulled down in 1893 and the ground built over, so that the address where three quarters of the critical philosophy was written is now a coordinate and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Kant's house on Prinzessinstraße taken before its demolition in 1893

stops.name: Königsberg, the answer about enlightenment
stops.date_confidence: attested to the December 1784 number of the Berlinische Monatsschrift; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Berlinische Monatsschrift has asked what enlightenment is. Kant answers in a few pages that it is a condition of persons rather than of an age, that the obstacle is not want of understanding but want of resolve, and that the free public use of reason by a scholar addressing a reading public must be allowed even where the private use, inside an office a man holds, is bound. He is a salaried professor of a Prussian king, writing this. The motto he gives it is two words of Horace. Ten years later the king's censor reads the essay back to him.
stops.quote: Sapere aude! Have courage to use your own reason! That is the motto of enlightenment.
stops.quote_source: An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?, 1784, English translation hosted on Wikisource
suggested_refs: Berlinische Monatsschrift, December 1784, pages 481 to 494
sources: Kant, Beantwortung der Frage: Was ist Aufklärung? (1784)

stops.name: Königsberg, the crooked timber
stops.date_confidence: attested to the November 1784 number of the Berlinische Monatsschrift; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In the same year he sets out nine propositions on universal history. Nature has planted in the species an unsociable sociability, an antagonism that is also the engine of every advance; the perfect civil constitution is the task nature has set, and no generation that works at it will see it finished. The sixth proposition concedes the material the whole scheme has to survive. Isaiah Berlin will later render the line as crooked timber and make it better known in English than it ever was in German; the quotation given here is de Quincey's, from the primary text.
stops.quote: Out of wood so crooked and perverse as that which man is made of, nothing absolutely straight can ever be wrought.
stops.quote_source: Idea of a Universal History on a Cosmopolitical Plan, Proposition the Sixth, trans. Thomas de Quincey, on Wikisource
suggested_refs: Idee zu einer allgemeinen Geschichte in weltbürgerlicher Absicht (1784), Sixth Proposition
sources: Kant, Idee zu einer allgemeinen Geschichte (1784)
de Quincey translation on Wikisource, fetched
Isaiah Berlin, The Crooked Timber of Humanity (1990), for the famous English rendering

stops.name: Königsberg, the Groundwork
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals is short, and it is the first book he writes about what to do. It looks for the supreme principle of morality not in happiness, not in the will of God and not in the consequences of an act, but in the form of a maxim that could be willed as a law for everyone. From that one test comes the demand that a human being never be used as a means only. A century later, in Manhattan, Felix Adler will build an ethical movement arguing past the categorical imperative toward what he calls the ethical manifold.
stops.quote: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.
stops.quote_source: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, 1785 (Project Gutenberg 5682)
suggested_refs: Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten, Riga, Hartknoch, 1785, first edition
sources: Kant, Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten (1785)

stops.name: Königsberg, the second edition of the first Critique
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He rewrites the Critique of Pure Reason for its second edition, replaces the deduction of the categories, adds a refutation of idealism, and writes a new preface that says in one sentence what the whole book was for. Speculative reason is confined to the world of appearance, and the confinement is not presented as a loss. God, freedom and immortality cannot be proved, and they cannot be disproved either; the ground vacated by proof is left standing empty for practical reason. Seven years later the Prussian censors decline the trade.
stops.quote: I must, therefore, abolish knowledge, to make room for belief.
stops.quote_source: Critique of Pure Reason, Preface to the Second Edition, trans. J.M.D. Meiklejohn (Project Gutenberg 4280)
suggested_refs: Kritik der reinen Vernunft, second edition, Riga, Hartknoch, 1787
sources: Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, 2nd ed. (1787)

stops.name: Königsberg, the Critique of Practical Reason
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The second Critique appears, and with it the doctrine that the moral law is a fact of reason, known not by inference from anything prior but in the consciousness of being bound by it. Freedom is not proved out of the world; it is the condition of a law we cannot deny we stand under. He serves his second term as Rector of the university in the same year, an office rotated among the senior professors. The conclusion of the book sets two objects side by side and declines to rank them.
stops.quote: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
stops.quote_source: Critique of Practical Reason, Conclusion, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott (Project Gutenberg 5683, line 6330)
suggested_refs: Kritik der praktischen Vernunft, Riga, Hartknoch, 1788
The same sentence, cut into Kant's memorial wall in Kaliningrad

stops.name: Königsberg, the Critique of the Power of Judgment
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The third Critique closes the system at the Prinzessinstraße house, nine years after the first opened it. It takes up two judgments neither earlier book could hold: that a thing is beautiful, which claims everyone's assent while resting on no concept, and that an organism is purposive, which we cannot help making and cannot cash as knowledge of nature. Between the realm of necessity and the realm of freedom he lays a bridge and calls it a bridge. He is sixty-six and has finished what the silent decade began.
suggested_refs: Kritik der Urteilskraft, Berlin and Libau, Lagarde und Friederich, 1790

stops.name: Tübingen, three students share a chamber
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the shared room at the Tübinger Stift, inherited from the atlas entry for Schelling
stops.campa: In October, seven hundred miles southwest of the study where the third Critique was finished, three theology students at the Tübinger Stift are put in one chamber: Hegel, Hölderlin, and Schelling, who is fifteen. They read Kant, Plato and Spinoza by candlelight. Nothing of Kant himself travels here; the books do the traveling, as they have travelled to Jena and Berlin and Leipzig. The old man in Königsberg has never seen the Neckar, will never see it, and is at this moment the common property of a room he could not find on a map without his own atlas.
suggested_refs: The Tübinger Stift chamber shared by Hegel, Hölderlin and Schelling from October 1790
sources: QUEUE.md, atlas entries for Hegel and Schelling

stops.name: Königsberg, Fichte at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the first interview, inherited from the atlas entry for Fichte
stops.campa: A penniless Saxon of twenty-nine arrives on foot and by coach and gets himself admitted to the old man's house on the fourth of July. Johann Gottlieb Fichte had opened the Critiques the summer before in Leipzig, tutoring a student in a philosophy he did not yet know, and had been struck as by lightning. The interview is cold. Fichte goes away and writes the Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation in a few weeks in order to be worth talking to, and Kant arranges its publication. It appears anonymously in 1792 and Germany reads it as Kant's fourth Critique.
suggested_refs: Versuch einer Kritik aller Offenbarung, Königsberg, 1792, published anonymously

stops.name: Jena, the book routed past the censor
stops.date_confidence: the 1792 censorship block and the 1793 Jena publication are attested; month and day of publication unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The Berlin censorship commission stops the second Piece of Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason in 1792. Kant does not fight the commission. He sends all four Pieces to the philosophy faculty at Jena, which is competent to license a book of philosophy, and the volume comes out complete in 1793 with the censor bypassed rather than beaten. In this same town Karl Leonhard Reinhold has been teaching the Critiques to students, among them Novalis; Schiller lectures here; Fichte will hold the chair within the year. Kant sets foot in none of it.
suggested_refs: Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft, Königsberg, Nicolovius, 1793
Reinhold's Briefe über die Kantische Philosophie, the vehicle of Kant's fame

stops.name: Königsberg, the royal order
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1794, following the second edition of the Religion; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: After the second edition of the Religion appears, the censor is angry enough to obtain a cabinet order under the king's own name. It accuses the professor of misusing his philosophy against the doctrines of scripture and requires him to write and lecture no further on religion. Kant is seventy. He complies, and the wording of his compliance is exact: as his majesty's most loyal subject, he will refrain. The pledge is made to a man and not to an office. Friedrich Wilhelm II dies in 1797, and Kant considers himself released, and says so in print.
suggested_refs: The cabinet order of Friedrich Wilhelm II, October 1794, and Kant's reply
sources: Kant, correspondence with the Prussian cabinet, October 1794, cited in Kuehn (2001)

stops.name: Königsberg, Perpetual Peace
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He writes a treaty. The form is deliberate: preliminary articles, definitive articles, a secret article, all laid out for signature by states with no intention of signing. No peace is valid that reserves the matter of a future war. Standing armies are to be abolished in time. No state is to be acquired by another by inheritance, exchange or purchase. The civil constitution of every state is to be republican. He is seventy-one, forbidden by his king to write about religion, and writing about war instead.
stops.quote: No conclusion of Peace shall be held to be valid as such, when it has been made with the secret reservation of the material for a future War.
stops.quote_source: Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch, First Section, Preliminary Article 1, English translation hosted on Wikisource
suggested_refs: Zum ewigen Frieden. Ein philosophischer Entwurf, Königsberg, Nicolovius, 1795

stops.name: Kneiphof, the last lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested year of retirement at seventy-two; the date of the final lecture is not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He gives his last lecture and ends a teaching career of forty-one years, the whole of it inside the building he entered at sixteen as a student. He has lectured on logic, metaphysics, ethics, natural law, anthropology, mathematics, physics and physical geography; he has described monsoons and currents and the customs of peoples he has never seen, to students who mostly will not see them either. He is seventy-two. The room empties and he walks home, which takes a few minutes.
suggested_refs: The Albertina lecture halls on the Kneiphof, Kant's only workplace for forty-one years

stops.name: Königsberg, the Metaphysics of Morals
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The Metaphysics of Morals appears in two parts, the doctrine of right and the doctrine of virtue: the whole ethical system worked downward from the principle the Groundwork had isolated twelve years earlier into property, contract, punishment, marriage, the duties a person owes himself, and the right of a state to go to war. The pure moral philosopher comes down at last to cases and finds them harder than the principle. He is seventy-three and writing with a hand that is beginning to fail him.
stops.quote: So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only.
stops.quote_source: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Second Section, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, 1785 (Project Gutenberg 5682); the formula the 1797 work applies to cases
suggested_refs: Die Metaphysik der Sitten, Königsberg, Nicolovius, 1797, in two parts

stops.name: Königsberg, the Conflict of the Faculties
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He publishes The Conflict of the Faculties, on the standing quarrel between the philosophy faculty, which has nothing to appeal to but reason, and the three higher faculties of theology, law and medicine, which answer to the government that licenses them. In the preface he prints the royal order of 1794, his own reply, and the reasoning by which a pledge given to a king expires with that king. The old man who obeyed in silence for four years had been keeping the paperwork the whole time.
suggested_refs: Der Streit der Fakultäten, Königsberg, Nicolovius, 1798, with the 1794 cabinet order printed in the preface

stops.name: Königsberg, the letter against Fichte
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1799; the open letter is the Erklärung in Beziehung auf Fichtes Wissenschaftslehre, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In August he prints a declaration concerning Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre and repudiates it entirely. The Critique of Pure Reason, he says, is to be taken by the letter, and he asks to be protected from his friends. Fichte at Jena had been building an idealism out of Kant's own distinction, with Schelling behind him and the Jena circle reading them both; the disciple who once walked to this door for an interview is now the successor everyone assumes. Kant will not have it. It is his last intervention in philosophy.
suggested_refs: Erklärung in Beziehung auf Fichtes Wissenschaftslehre, August 1799

segments.name: The Walk, and the Sea Not Seen

stops.name: Königsberg, the Philosophengang
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the walk belongs to the 1780s and 1790s with no datable event, and the clock-setting story is legend rather than documented practice
stops.campa: A tree-lined walk on the old city rampart is named the Philosophengang after him, and the legend runs that his afternoon walk along it was so exact that the neighbors set their clocks by him. Heine put the story into print in 1834, thirty years after the man was dead, and it has not been out of print since. There is a second half: that he missed the walk once, for Rousseau's Emile or for the news from France, and the tellings do not agree which. None of it is documented and all of it is repeated. It is the only image of Kant most people carry.
suggested_refs: Heine, Zur Geschichte der Religion und Philosophie in Deutschland (1834), the source of the clock legend
sources: popular biographical tradition, flagged as tradition

stops.name: Pillau, the road not taken
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition; the absence of a coastal visit is inferred from the silence of the letters and the biographers, and the date is a placeholder inside the professorship years
stops.campa: Königsberg is a Baltic port, and the open sea lies some forty kilometers down the Pregel and the Frisches Haff at Pillau. Kant lectured on physical geography for four decades, on tides and currents and the ice of the far north, and no letter, no diary and no biographer records his going to look at open water. The absence is not a document. It is a silence in the record, offered here as silence: the man who systematized the whole globe from a study may or may not once have stood on a shore.
suggested_refs: The road from Königsberg to Pillau, about forty kilometers, along the Frisches Haff
sources: Manfred Geier, Kants Welt (2003), for the tradition

stops.name: Königsberg, the Opus Postumum
stops.date_confidence: the decline and the unfinished manuscript are attested to the last years; no single date, defaulted to 1800-01-01
stops.campa: His memory goes first for recent things, then for names, then for the thread of a sentence. He goes on working. The manuscript he leaves attempts to close a gap he has come to think fatal, between the metaphysical foundations of natural science and physics itself, and it circles the same problem sheet after sheet with the handwriting deteriorating across the pages. It is printed long after his death as the Opus Postumum. The system built in eleven years of silence does not close.
suggested_refs: The Opus Postumum manuscript sheets, Akademie-Ausgabe volumes 21 and 22

stops.name: Königsberg, the death on Prinzessinstraße
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is corrected to the Prinzessinstraße house, the earlier figure having fallen about four kilometers west of the historic city
stops.campa: He dies in his own house, attended by his servant and a few friends, seventy-nine years and ten months old, after years of physical and mental decline. Wasianski, the former student who has run the household through the last of it, writes down the final coherent words: es ist gut, it is good. He has died something under two miles from the room where he was born, in the same city, in the only country he ever saw. Every place his books had by then reached is a place he had never been.
stops.quote_source: Reported last words, in Wasianski, Immanuel Kant in seinen letzten Lebensjahren (1804)

stops.name: Königsberg Cathedral, the procession and the vault
stops.date_confidence: burial attested to 28 February 1804; the procession is attested to the same month, and the sixteen-day interval between death and burial is arithmetic, its cause not given by the sources consulted
stops.campa: The body lies in state and is carried through the streets in a funeral procession that contemporaries call the largest Königsberg has given a private citizen. Sixteen days pass between the death and the burial, and the sources consulted do not say why. He is laid in the Professorengewölbe at the northeast end of the cathedral, the vault the Albertina keeps for its faculty, so that the men lying around him taught the men who taught him. It is three hundred meters from the hall where he matriculated at sixteen.

stops.name: Königsberg, the Rauch bronze unveiled
stops.date_confidence: attested date of unveiling; the coordinate for the Kantberg site at Prinzessinstraße and Altstädtische Bergstraße is approximate
stops.campa: Christian Daniel Rauch works on a bronze Kant in his last years; Hermann Gladenbeck casts it in Berlin in 1857, the year Rauch dies. Seven years pass between the casting and the unveiling. The city sets it up on the eighteenth of October 1864 on the Kantberg, where Prinzessinstraße meets the Altstädtische Bergstraße, a few doors from the house he died in, and moves it in 1885 to the Paradeplatz southwest of the university. It is the first public image of him in the town that kept him for seventy-nine years.
suggested_refs: Christian Daniel Rauch's Kant monument, cast by Gladenbeck 1857, unveiled 18 October 1864
sources: de.wikipedia.org, article on the Kant monument in Königsberg

stops.name: Königsberg Cathedral, the grave moved outside
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the move; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The remains are taken out of the cathedral and put in a neo-Gothic chapel built against the northeast corner of the building. The move and the year are firm. Two things often said about it are not. The chapel was not called the Stoa Kantiana, which is the name of the structure that replaces it in 1924, and the claim that it was commissioned for the centenary of the Critique of Pure Reason is confirmed by no source reached in this research. What is certain is that Kant is now outside the wall, in a structure of his own, visible from the street.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the 1880 neo-Gothic burial chapel at the cathedral's northeast corner

stops.name: Königsberg, the colonnade of Friedrich Lahrs
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1924 bicentenary; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: For the bicentenary of the birth, Friedrich Lahrs builds an open colonnade of Rochlitz porphyry over the grave at the choir end, replacing the decayed chapel of 1880: a hall of pillars around a slab, effectively roofless. German sources call the monument a cenotaph and record that the remains were reburied more than once. Whether what lies under the slab is all of what was buried in 1804 is a question the documentation does not close, and it is not closed here either.
suggested_refs: The Stoa Kantiana of Friedrich Lahrs, 1924, in Rochlitz porphyry

stops.name: Königsberg, the bombing and the buried statue
stops.date_confidence: RAF raids attested to late August 1944; the burial of the statue is attested to 1944 without a day, defaulted to 08-01
stops.campa: RAF bombers burn out the cathedral in the last days of August. The spire and roof go and the shell stands open to the sky for half a century. The Kantiana collection of the city museum, everything of his the town had kept, is destroyed with the building that held it. Ahead of the Red Army the Rauch bronze is carted to the park of Schloss Friedrichstein and buried, and it has never been found, though it has been looked for hard. The colonnade at the choir end survives the bombing, the siege, and the Soviet demolition of the old city around it.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the gutted Königsberg Cathedral, 1945 to 1990, with Kant's colonnade intact beside it
sources: de.wikipedia.org, article on the Kant monument

stops.name: Kaliningrad, the Haacke replica
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the ceremonial erection; the coordinate is the university main building on Universitetskaya Street
stops.campa: Marion Gräfin Dönhoff, born in East Prussia and driven out of it, commissions with the ZEIT-Stiftung and Friedrich Wilhelm Christians a new Kant from the sculptor Harald Haacke, and on the twenty-seventh of June it is set up beside the New Albertina on Universitetskaya Street. It is a replica and not a recast; the mould Gladenbeck used is not what stands here, and the description that calls it cast from surviving German moulds should be checked before it is repeated. Forty-seven years after the city stopped being German, the philosopher is back on the pavement outside his university.
suggested_refs: Harald Haacke's Kant, erected 27 June 1992 beside the New Albertina, Kaliningrad

stops.name: Wiener Neustadt, the Critique bound inside a schoolbook
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the source gives the episode as undated, at about age fifteen, and the year here is inferred from Steiner's birth in 1861
stops.campa: A boy of about fifteen buys the Critique of Pure Reason in a bookshop in Wiener Neustadt, takes the volume apart, and binds its pages inside his school history book so that he can read it through the history lesson. Some pages he reads more than twenty times. Rudolf Steiner will spend a career arguing against what he calls Kant's barrier. He is not alone at the desk: Nietzsche reads Kant by night at Leipzig against the philology of his days, Jung reads him by night at Basel, and in Copenhagen the Bohr household's Friday talk runs from Kant to the physiology of respiration.
suggested_refs: Steiner's account of reading Kant inside his history textbook, in his autobiography

stops.name: Kaliningrad, the name, the paint, the flowers
stops.date_confidence: the 2005 renaming, the 2010 renaming and the 2018 vandalism are each attested to the year; the stop is anchored at 2005 and runs forward
stops.campa: At the celebration of the city's 750th anniversary, counted from Königsberg, Vladimir Putin and Gerhard Schröder announce that the university will be renamed Immanuel Kant State University of Russia; in 2010 it is renamed again, Immanuel Kant Baltic Federal University. In 2018, during a campaign to give his name to the airport, unknown hands throw pink paint over the tomb and over the statue. The paint comes off. Newlyweds in Kaliningrad go on bringing flowers to the colonnade at the choir end. He has not moved. Everyone else has come to him.
